title: Salute to Women in Jazz, Cobi Narita and playing on Broadway
summary: At a women-in-jazz week the club owner locked out the group, so they played in the street at 53rd and Broadway.

blocks.x: We should -- I wish you had played it when you did that Women In Jazz Festival here in New York.
Yeah.
During the first week in June.
Well --
As you say, you just had a trio with you (inaudible).
Last year, you know when Cobi had the Salute To Women In Jazz, and they got locked out on the street? (1979)
Yes. This is -- let's get the name right -- Cobi Narita.
Yeah, Cobi Narita is Salute To Women In Jazz. She's the --
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. W/Orth 2-2915 W/Orth 2-2943
Just let me spell it.
Yeah.
It's C-o-b-i, the first name. And the second name is N-a-r-i-t-a.
Cobi is the director of the Universal Jazz Coalition. And her emphasis is on promoting female jazz musicians.
So anyway, I was selected as one of the honorees, because she had Mary Lou Williams and --
Somebody else from Pittsburgh, incidentally.
Yes. Mary Lou and myself and some other women in jazz -- not necessarily performers.
Joyce Wein was one of the recipients and -- I forgot who else.
Anyway, they were -- they had booked the room -- I don't know what they call it now -- but it the former Birdland.
And they had arranged for this to be a whole week of jazz for women. And they had two

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.
WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
some nights in the club, and for/reason or other, the owner locked them out the third night.
Oh yes, you were telling me this.
It seemed that --
He wanted a bigger cut of the action?
I imagine the original arrangement was, I thought he was doing a goodwill gesture by letting them use the place.
But then business was so good, that he decided that he wanted a piece of the action. And because Cobi wanted to hold him to his original agreement which there wasn't to going to be much money anyway.
They couldn't come to -- so he locked the group out. So they performed on Broadway -- 53rd and Broadway -- outdoors.
Out on the street.
Out on the street.
And we drew quite a large audience. I sang, of course, and I had brought my
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
horn along. So Nancy Pratt is a female trumpet player, and so I was over there talking to her, and I brought my horn out and showed it to her.
So I said, 'If you play, I'll play,' one of those kind of things.
So we got out there and I played my horn on 53rd and Broadway in full view of the audience.
But now I'm anxious to really get a solo on wax -- you know, on record. And then I'll really be identified as a trumpet player.
Oh, I think it's long overdue from what you've been through.
Yeah. I think I can do it. I mean, the guys encourages me. And ev@rytime I pull it out, I play my little few notes, they sort of sit up and take notice.
So I think I'm feeling a little bit more secure than I did at the beginning. I'm going to learn a real -- I promised myself and a lot of other people that I'm going to learn a real good solo. And
